lessons.title: SI quantities, prefixes, and engineering notation
lessons.objective: Identify quantity and unit roles, interpret case-sensitive SI prefixes, and convert exact values between scientific, engineering, and prefixed notation.
scope: Seven SI base quantities and selected electrical derived units
Common prefixes pico through tera, plus centi and deci; full current BIPM table linked
Case-sensitive symbols, the special kilogram naming convention, and no stacked prefixes
Normalized scientific notation versus an explicitly defined engineering notation convention
Conversion preserves physical value and does not create measurement precision
workedExamples: Separate the numerical value, prefix, and unit in 2.4 kΩ; distinguish current A from charge C=A s
Compare 1 mV with 1 MV: (1 MV)/(1 mV) is 10^9
Convert 4.7 μF to 4.7×10^-6 F
Convert 3300 pF to 3.3 nF
Represent 0.000082 V as 8.2×10^-5 V and 82×10^-6 V
Convert the stated 0.0200 A to 20.0 mA without losing its three significant figures
lessons.guided: Convert a capacitance from nF to F and pF, then distinguish milli from mega without changing the quantity.

interaction.purpose: Choose a base quantity and two prefixes. Predict the converted value and direction of numerical change, then inspect an exact scale table and reverse conversion.

mistakes: Treat m and M as interchangeable
Ignore symbol case
Expand both into powers of ten and compare.
Reverse the conversion direction
Confuse unit size and numerical count
A smaller target unit needs more units for the same quantity.
Normalize every notation coefficient below ten
Confuse engineering with scientific convention
Use 1<=|a|<1000 and exponent divisible by three for the stated engineering convention.
Infer extra accuracy after conversion
Confuse exact scaling with new information
Preserve the original measurement's reporting precision.
lessons.acceptance: Required questions check both prefix case and general scaling, engineering normalization, and quantity/unit identification. Reuse scientific-notation source questions under separate F06 identity.

lessons.title: Conversions with powers, rates, and offsets
lessons.objective: Convert signed quantities, areas, volumes, inverse units, and compound rates with explicit unit cancellation, and distinguish temperature values from temperature differences.
scope: Exact equal-quantity conversion factors
Squared, cubed, and inverse unit scales
Compound units including speed, density, and voltage/time slopes
Celsius and kelvin values versus differences using the exact offset
Physical quantities unchanged under a consistent conversion
workedExamples: Convert a signed offset -750 ms to -3/4 s
Convert 2.5 cm² to 0.00025 m² by squaring the length factor
Convert 4 mm³ to 4×10^-9 m³ by cubing the length factor
Convert 72 km/h to 20 m/s with both numerator and denominator factors
Convert 1.2 g/cm³ to 1200 kg/m³
Convert 25 °C to 298.15 K but a difference of 25 °C to 25 K
lessons.guided: Convert a small area and a voltage-change rate while retaining the power and denominator conversions.

interaction.purpose: Change a length-unit power among 1,2,3,-1 and predict the full scale factor. Show factor cancellation and a labeled table; compare area conversion with conversion of a side length.

mistakes: Apply a length factor once to area or volume
Ignore the unit exponent
Raise the entire conversion factor to the same power.
Multiply a denominator scale in the wrong direction
Lose unit cancellation
Write the desired unit in the numerator of its conversion factor before simplifying.
Drop the sign of an offset
Assume all measurements are positive magnitudes
Convert the signed coordinate with the same positive scale factor.
Add 273.15 to a temperature difference
Confuse an affine value conversion with an interval
Subtract two converted values and observe cancellation of the common offset.
lessons.acceptance: Four checkpoint questions include all three nontrivial unit powers, compound conversions, absolute/difference temperature cases, and valid versus invalid cancellation reasoning. Basic millisecond/meter conversions retain source-family answer rules.

lessons.title: Dimensional checks and model parameters
lessons.objective: Determine mechanical and electrical dimensions, check every term and function argument in an equation, and infer parameter units while recognizing what dimensional analysis cannot prove.
scope: Dimensions versus particular units
Exponent bookkeeping for mass, length, time, and electric current
Mechanical and selected electrical derived units with supplied defining relationships
Additive homogeneity and dimensionless log, exponential, and trigonometric inputs
Parameter units in polynomial, exponential, and oscillatory models
Dimensional consistency is necessary but does not fix dimensionless coefficients or prove physical validity
workedExamples: From F=m a infer force dimensions M L T^-2
From power=energy/time and voltage=power/current infer voltage dimensions M L² T^-3 I^-1
From R=V/I infer resistance dimensions M L² T^-3 I^-2
Compare x=v t+(1/2)a t² with x=v t²+a t; audit every term
For exp(-t/tau), infer tau has time dimensions and k in exp(k t) has reciprocal-time dimensions
For x(t)=a0+a1 t+a2 t² infer each coefficient's units; explain why x=2v t can pass dimensions without being a validated model
lessons.guided: Build a resistance dimension vector from supplied power and voltage definitions, then identify a valid dimensionless time ratio.

interaction.purpose: Choose powers p,q in v^p t^q and a dimensionless coefficient. Predict length/time exponents and whether the expression can represent length. Compare the term-dimension table and explain why changing the coefficient preserves dimensions.

mistakes: Add quantities with incompatible dimensions
Focus only on numerical arithmetic
Compare each additive term separately.
Place a dimensional time directly in exp or log
Omit a rate or reference
Construct a same-dimension ratio or rate-times-time product.
Give every coefficient the output unit
Ignore powers of the input
Divide output dimensions by the accompanying input power.
Treat a passed check as proof
Confuse necessary with sufficient conditions
Test or derive dimensionless coefficients and model assumptions separately.
lessons.acceptance: Checkpoint questions require an electrical dimension vector, both valid and invalid equation judgments with a limitation check, exponential parameter units, and dimensionless-argument decisions. Definitions are supplied rather than assuming prior circuit instruction.

lessons.title: Significant figures and deliberate rounding
lessons.objective: Interpret stated measurement precision, round using an explicit convention, and apply addition and multiplication reporting rules without allowing exact counts or conversions to limit precision.
scope: Leading, internal, and trailing zeros; explicit scientific notation
Ambiguous trailing zeros in bare integers; exact counts and definitions
Rounding places versus significant digits
Nearest rounding with exact ties away from zero, explicitly stated for these exercises
Addition/subtraction by last place; multiplication/division by significant-digit count
Guard digits and final rounding; reporting precision is not a complete uncertainty analysis
workedExamples: Count four significant digits in 0.004050; explain why bare 1200 needs more context and an exact count does not impose a finite precision limit
Round 6.275 to hundredths as 6.28 under the stated tie convention
Round 9.9995 to four significant digits as 10.00, preserving its final place
Report 12.11+0.3 as 12.4 because tenths is the coarsest input place
Report 2.34×1.2 as 2.8 to two significant digits
Convert measured 4.56 m to 456 cm; exact 100 cm/m does not reduce precision
Track precision through (1.26+2.1)×2.45: keep 3.36 internally and report 8.2; prematurely using 3.4 would give 8.3
lessons.guided: Count digits, select a report with the requested trailing zeros, and round a product only after computing its full value.

interaction.purpose: Enter an exact finite decimal and choose significant digits or decimal places. Predict the rounded numerical value and a precision-preserving report, then compare the rounding step and nearby values. Include ties, negative inputs, and carry across a power of ten.

mistakes: Count leading zeros as measured digits
Confuse decimal placeholders with recorded precision
Start at the first nonzero digit and include meaningful trailing decimal zeros.
Apply the fewest-digit rule to addition
Confuse significant digits with decimal places
Align the final reported place for sums and differences.
Discard trailing zeros from a requested report
Preserve value but lose stated precision
Use explicit decimal or scientific notation showing the last reported place.
Treat exact conversion factors as uncertain measurements
Infer uncertainty from a short written constant
Exact definitions and counts do not limit significant figures.
Round at every step
Lose guard digits
Track the reporting constraint separately, then round once.
lessons.acceptance: Questions independently assess counts and ambiguity, a carry case with explicit precision, and both reporting-operation classes. Numeric equivalence is graded separately from the display choice, preserving trailing-zero meaning without adding a text-format grader.

lessons.title: Measurement resolution, uncertainty, and bounds
lessons.objective: Distinguish resolution, repeatability, discrepancy, and uncertainty; interpret stated bounds and relative uncertainty; and propagate simple bounds without inventing a confidence level.
scope: Read labeled scale increments and digital resolution
Resolution alone does not establish accuracy or total uncertainty
Repeatability versus discrepancy from a stated reference
Explicit symmetric bounds, inclusive endpoints, and unit conversion
Relative and percent uncertainty for nonzero nominal values; zero nominal case
Exact interval propagation for sums, differences, scales, and positive products/quotients
Uncertainty sources beyond repeated scatter; interval compatibility is not proof
workedExamples: A display 1.20 V with 0.01 V resolution has a conservative rounding-only bound ±0.005 V under the stated ideal nearest-step model; this is not total instrument uncertainty
Interpret 2.50±0.05 V as a stated bound [2.45,2.55] V and 2% relative uncertainty
Compare 9.99,10.00,10.01 with 10.49,10.50,10.51 against reference 10.00: same range, different mean discrepancy
Propagate stated bounds in (12±0.2)-(5±0.1) to [6.7,7.3]
Propagate (3±0.1)(2±0.1) to [5.51,6.51], showing asymmetric deviations from nominal 6
Check an inclusive boundary reference 10.2 against [9.8,10.2], while explaining that compatibility does not prove the measurement exact
For nominal zero with ±0.1 V bounds, retain the valid absolute interval but report relative uncertainty as undefined
lessons.guided: Convert a nominal measurement and its bound together, compute percent uncertainty, and check a reference against the inclusive interval.

interaction.purpose: Change a displayed scale reading, resolution, and stated additional bound. Predict the conservative interval and compare a reference using keyboard controls. Show a labeled scale and equivalent numeric table; distinguish a tighter resolution from evidence of accuracy.

mistakes: Treat extra display digits as accuracy
Confuse resolution and bias
Compare with a stated reference and account for specifications.
Use a difference from reference as uncertainty
Mix discrepancy with estimated dispersion or bounds
Keep the reference discrepancy and uncertainty statement separate.
Assume every plus/minus means a 95% interval
Invent an unstated probability model
Read the supplied bound definition; a confidence level needs additional information.
Convert the central value but not its uncertainty
Scale only half the report
Apply the same exact unit factor to both.
Cancel uncertainties in a subtraction
Confuse signed changes with possible bounds
Subtract the opposite endpoints to find the minimum and maximum.
Divide a bound by a zero nominal value
Force a relative percentage
Keep the absolute bound and say the requested relative measure is undefined.
lessons.acceptance: Checkpoint coverage includes scale/resolution interpretation, repeatability versus reference discrepancy, bounds with conversion and percent/zero cases, and propagated sum/product or quotient bounds. All probability claims are excluded unless supplied; the fuller NIST guidance is linked for later study.
